Propensity Score Adjustment in ForestSearch: Complete Workflow

IPTW vs. DR G-Computation — Implementation, Theory, and Simulation Evaluation

Larry F. León

Published

March 25, 2026

1 Methodology

1.1 Two Approaches to PS Adjustment

ForestSearch offers two PS adjustment methods for GLM effect estimation in observational studies. Both use propensity scores estimated on the full sample; they differ in how the PS enters the outcome model.

1.1.1 Option A: Stabilized IPTW (Default)

Inverse probability of treatment weighting creates a pseudo-population where treatment is independent of measured confounders. Stabilized weights are:

\[ \text{sw}_i = \begin{cases} P(W=1) / \hat{e}(X_i) & \text{if } W_i = 1 \\ P(W=0) / (1 - \hat{e}(X_i)) & \text{if } W_i = 0 \end{cases} \]

The outcome model is simply glm(Y ~ treat, weights = sw, ...). The treatment coefficient is the marginal causal effect — no post-processing required.

1.1.2 Option B: Bang & Robins (2005) DR G-Computation

The doubly-robust approach from Section 2.2 of Bang & Robins (2005) adds the inverse probability of treatment received as a covariate:

\[ \frac{1}{f(W_i \mid V; \hat\alpha)} = \begin{cases} 1 / \hat{e}(X_i) & \text{if } W_i = 1 \\ 1 / (1 - \hat{e}(X_i)) & \text{if } W_i = 0 \end{cases} \]

The outcome model is glm(Y ~ treat + ips_covar, ...).

Critically, for non-identity links (logit, log), the treatment coefficient \(\hat\beta_1\) is not the DR treatment effect. Section 2.2 of Bang & Robins (2005) specifies:

\[ \hat\mu_{dr} = n^{-1} \sum_i \bigl[e(1, V_i; \hat\beta, \hat\phi) - e(0, V_i; \hat\beta, \hat\phi)\bigr] \]

This requires G-computation: predicting under both counterfactual treatment assignments, with the IPS covariate set to its correct value under each assignment (\(1/\hat{e}(X)\) for \(W=1\), \(1/(1-\hat{e}(X))\) for \(W=0\)), then averaging the contrast.

1.1.3 Key Theoretical Distinction

The DR property requires that the outcome model s(W, V; beta) contain confounders. If either the PS model or the outcome model for \(E(Y \mid W, V)\) is correctly specified, the estimator is consistent.

ForestSearch’s estimator closures intentionally use treatment-only outcome models within subgroup slices (no confounders in the outcome model). This means:

  • IPTW: Works correctly. The weights create a pseudo-population; no confounders needed in the outcome model.
  • DR G-comp: Loses its doubly-robust property because confounders are omitted from the outcome model. Reduces to a misspecified regression with the IPS covariate, which has no theoretical guarantee.

This document demonstrates this distinction empirically.

1.2 Comparison Summary

Property IPTW (Option A) DR G-comp (Option B)
Model glm(Y ~ treat, weights = sw) glm(Y ~ treat + ips_covar) + G-comp
Coefficient IS the effect Requires G-computation
Requires confounders in outcome model? No Yes (for DR property)
Works with ForestSearch’s treatment-only models? Yes No
Extreme PS sensitivity Moderate (stabilized) Low (covariate)
Reference Hernán & Robins (2020) Bang & Robins (2005), §2.2

2 Complete Workflow

2.1 Stage 1: GRF Screening (Internal PS)

When use_grf = TRUE, GRF fits causal_forest(X, Y, W) which internally estimates \(\hat{e}(X_i) = E[W_i \mid X_i]\) via regression_forest(X, W). These out-of-bag, cross-fitted propensity scores are used within GRF for CATE estimation only — they do not affect downstream effect estimates.

2.2 Stage 2: PS Estimation for Effect Adjustment

Location: forestsearch_main.R, Section 2C

After outcome type is resolved (Section 2B), ForestSearch optionally estimates propensity scores on the full df.analysis.

forestsearch(..., ps_method = "grf", ps_adjust_method = "iptw")
     ↓
  Section 2C: estimate_propensity_scores()
     ├── Estimate e(X) on full sample
     ├── Trim PS to [2.5%, 97.5%]
     ├── Compute stabilized weights: sw = P(W)/e(X) or P(1-W)/(1-e(X))
     ├── Compute IPS covariate:       1/e(X) or 1/(1-e(X))
     ├── Add ps_hat, sw, ips_covar columns to df.analysis
     └── Rebuild estimator closure:
           make_effect_estimator(..., ps_adjust_method = "iptw")

Default behavior:

Setting ps_method ps_adjust_method Rationale
is.RCT = TRUE "none" N/A Randomization ensures balance
is.RCT = FALSE "grf" "iptw" Non-parametric PS, stabilized weights
User-supplied ps_hat = vec "iptw" Maximum flexibility

2.3 Stage 3: Subgroup Search

The estimator closure is called on each candidate subgroup slice. For IPTW, the stabilized weights computed on the full sample are carried into each slice. The weights are never re-estimated within subgroup slices.

2.4 Stage 4: Bootstrap

Bootstrap re-enters Section 2C on resampled data. The full estimation procedure (PS estimation → weight computation → estimator rebuild) is replicated from scratch on each bootstrap sample.

4 Simulation Study

4.1 Data-Generating Mechanism

simulate_obs_study <- function(
    n = 2000, seed = 42L,
    confounding_strength = 1.0,
    subgroup_effect = 0.8,       # log-OR in subgroup (harm)
    complement_effect = -0.4,    # log-OR in complement (benefit)
    prognostic_strength = 0.5,
    n_noise = 3
) {
  set.seed(seed)

  x1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)       # subgroup definer
  x2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)       # noise binary
  x3 <- rnorm(n)                 # confounder (treatment AND outcome)
  x4 <- rnorm(n)                 # prognostic only
  noise <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_noise), n, n_noise)
  colnames(noise) <- paste0("noise", seq_len(n_noise))

  # Confounded treatment: depends on x1 and x3
  lp_treat <- -0.5 + confounding_strength *
    (0.6 * x1 + 0.8 * x3 + 0.2 * x1 * x3)
  ps_true <- plogis(lp_treat)
  treat <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_true)

  in_sg <- x1 == 1

  # Outcome: x3 is a prognostic confounder
  lp_outcome <- -1.0 +
    prognostic_strength * x3 +
    0.3 * x4 +
    ifelse(in_sg, subgroup_effect, complement_effect) * treat
  event <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_outcome))

  tte <- rexp(n, rate = 0.05) + 1

  df <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n), x1 = x1, x2 = x2, x3 = x3, x4 = x4,
    treat = treat, event = event, tte = tte,
    in_sg = in_sg, ps_true = ps_true
  )
  cbind(df, noise)
}

4.2 Scenario Definitions

Seven scenarios spanning moderate to extreme confounding, weak to strong signals, sparse to dense covariate spaces, and a small-sample stress test.

scenarios <- list(
  A = list(
    name = "Moderate confounding",
    confounding_strength = 0.8, subgroup_effect = 0.8,
    complement_effect = -0.4, prognostic_strength = 0.5, n_noise = 3
  ),
  B = list(
    name = "Strong confounding",
    confounding_strength = 1.5, subgroup_effect = 0.8,
    complement_effect = -0.4, prognostic_strength = 0.8, n_noise = 3
  ),
  C = list(
    name = "Very strong confounding + weak signal",
    confounding_strength = 2.0, subgroup_effect = 0.5,
    complement_effect = -0.2, prognostic_strength = 1.0, n_noise = 3
  ),
  D = list(
    name = "Strong confounding + many noise covariates",
    confounding_strength = 1.5, subgroup_effect = 0.8,
    complement_effect = -0.4, prognostic_strength = 0.8, n_noise = 10
  ),
  E = list(
    name = "No confounding (RCT benchmark)",
    confounding_strength = 0.0, subgroup_effect = 0.8,
    complement_effect = -0.4, prognostic_strength = 0.5, n_noise = 3
  ),
  F_ = list(
    name = "Extreme confounding + strong signal",
    confounding_strength = 2.5, subgroup_effect = 1.2,
    complement_effect = -0.6, prognostic_strength = 1.2, n_noise = 3
  ),
  G = list(
    name = "Moderate confounding + small N",
    confounding_strength = 1.0, subgroup_effect = 0.8,
    complement_effect = -0.4, prognostic_strength = 0.5, n_noise = 3
  )
)

4.3 Monte Carlo Evaluation

Each scenario is evaluated with 200 Monte Carlo replications (N = 2000 per simulation, except Scenario G which uses N = 500).

Four estimators are compared:

  1. Unadjusted: glm(event ~ treat, family = binomial).
  2. IPTW (GRF PS): Stabilized weights from GRF-estimated PS.
  3. DR G-comp (GRF PS): Bang & Robins IPS covariate + G-computation.
  4. IPTW (Oracle PS): Stabilized weights from the true PS (benchmark).
Show code 
n_sims <- 200

confs_sim <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4")

run_mc <- function(scenario, n_sims, n_per_sim = 2000) {
  results <- data.frame(
    sim = integer(), method = character(),
    sg_est = numeric(), co_est = numeric(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  all_confs <- c(confs_sim, paste0("noise", seq_len(scenario$n_noise)))

  fn_none <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
    effect_measure = "OR", ps_adjust_method = "none")
  fn_iptw <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
    effect_measure = "OR", ps_adjust_method = "iptw")
  fn_dr   <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
    effect_measure = "OR", ps_adjust_method = "dr_gcomp")

  for (s in seq_len(n_sims)) {
    df_s <- simulate_obs_study(
      n = n_per_sim, seed = s,
      confounding_strength  = scenario$confounding_strength,
      subgroup_effect       = scenario$subgroup_effect,
      complement_effect     = scenario$complement_effect,
      prognostic_strength   = scenario$prognostic_strength,
      n_noise               = scenario$n_noise
    )

    ps_s <- estimate_propensity_scores(df_s, "treat", all_confs, method = "grf")
    df_s <- ps_s$data

    # Oracle IPTW weights
    p_treat <- mean(df_s$treat)
    df_s$sw_oracle <- ifelse(
      df_s$treat == 1,
      p_treat / df_s$ps_true,
      (1 - p_treat) / (1 - df_s$ps_true))

    sg <- df_s[df_s$x1 == 1, ]
    co <- df_s[df_s$x1 == 0, ]

    sg_orac <- sg; sg_orac$sw <- sg_orac$sw_oracle
    co_orac <- co; co_orac$sw <- co_orac$sw_oracle

    results <- rbind(results,
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "1. Unadjusted",
        sg_est = fn_none(sg)$estimate, co_est = fn_none(co)$estimate),
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "2. IPTW (GRF PS)",
        sg_est = fn_iptw(sg)$estimate, co_est = fn_iptw(co)$estimate),
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "3. DR G-comp (GRF PS)",
        sg_est = fn_dr(sg)$estimate, co_est = fn_dr(co)$estimate),
      data.frame(sim = s, method = "4. IPTW (Oracle PS)",
        sg_est = fn_iptw(sg_orac)$estimate, co_est = fn_iptw(co_orac)$estimate)
    )
  }
  results
}

all_results <- list()
for (sc_name in names(scenarios)) {
  sc <- scenarios[[sc_name]]
  cat("Running scenario", sc_name, ":", sc$name, "...\n")
  n_per <- if (sc_name == "G") 500 else 2000
  all_results[[sc_name]] <- run_mc(sc, n_sims, n_per_sim = n_per)
}

4.4 Results Summary

Show code 
summarize_scenario <- function(results, true_sg, true_co, scenario_name) {
  methods <- unique(results$method)
  rows <- list()
  for (m in methods) {
    sg <- results$sg_est[results$method == m]
    co <- results$co_est[results$method == m]
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      Scenario = scenario_name,
      Method = m,
      SG_Mean  = round(mean(sg, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      SG_Bias  = round(mean(sg, na.rm = TRUE) - true_sg, 3),
      SG_RMSE  = round(sqrt(mean((sg - true_sg)^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 3),
      CO_Mean  = round(mean(co, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      CO_Bias  = round(mean(co, na.rm = TRUE) - true_co, 3),
      CO_RMSE  = round(sqrt(mean((co - true_co)^2, na.rm = TRUE)), 3),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

summary_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(scenarios), function(sc) {
  sc_def <- scenarios[[sc]]
  summarize_scenario(
    all_results[[sc]],
    true_sg = sc_def$subgroup_effect,
    true_co = sc_def$complement_effect,
    scenario_name = paste0(sc, ": ", sc_def$name)
  )
}))

5 Why DR G-Computation Fails in ForestSearch

5.1 Theoretical Explanation

The Bang & Robins (2005) DR estimator from Section 2.2 fits:

\[ e(\Delta, V; \beta, \phi) = \Psi\bigl[s(\Delta, V; \beta) + \phi \cdot \{f(\Delta \mid V; \hat\alpha)\}^{-1}\bigr] \]

The doubly-robust property holds because \(\hat\mu_{dr}\) is consistent if either:

  1. The PS model \(\pi(V; \alpha)\) is correct, OR
  2. The outcome regression \(s(\Delta, V; \beta)\) is correct.

In ForestSearch, the outcome model within subgroup slices is intentionally Y ~ treat (no confounders), so condition (2) is never satisfied. When \(s(\Delta, V; \beta) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \Delta\) (no confounders), the IPS covariate \(\phi \cdot \{f(\Delta \mid V; \hat\alpha)\}^{-1}\) alone cannot absorb the confounding because \(\phi\) is a single scalar applied to a single covariate — it cannot adjust for the complex relationship between confounders and outcome.

IPTW, by contrast, does not require confounders in the outcome model. The weights directly create a pseudo-population where \(W \perp X\), so even a simple Y ~ treat model yields a consistent estimate.

5.2 Empirical Demonstration

set.seed(42)
n <- 5000
x1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
x3 <- rnorm(n)
ps_true <- plogis(-0.5 + 1.5 * (0.6 * x1 + 0.8 * x3))
treat <- rbinom(n, 1, ps_true)
lp <- -1.0 + 0.5 * x3 + ifelse(x1 == 1, 0.8, -0.4) * treat
event <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp))
df_demo <- data.frame(x1 = x1, x3 = x3, treat = treat, event = event)

ps_res <- estimate_propensity_scores(df_demo, "treat", c("x1", "x3"),
                                     method = "grf")
df_demo <- ps_res$data

fn_none <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
  effect_measure = "OR", ps_adjust_method = "none")
fn_iptw <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
  effect_measure = "OR", ps_adjust_method = "iptw")
fn_dr   <- make_effect_estimator("binary", "treat", "event",
  effect_measure = "OR", ps_adjust_method = "dr_gcomp")

sg <- df_demo[df_demo$x1 == 1, ]
co <- df_demo[df_demo$x1 == 0, ]

cat("=== N = 5000, strong confounding ===\n\n")
#> === N = 5000, strong confounding ===
cat("Subgroup {x1=1} — true log-OR = 0.80:\n")
#> Subgroup {x1=1} — true log-OR = 0.80:
cat(sprintf("  Unadjusted: %.3f (OR = %.2f)\n",
    fn_none(sg)$estimate, exp(fn_none(sg)$estimate)))
#>   Unadjusted: 1.324 (OR = 3.76)
cat(sprintf("  IPTW:       %.3f (OR = %.2f)\n",
    fn_iptw(sg)$estimate, exp(fn_iptw(sg)$estimate)))
#>   IPTW:       0.889 (OR = 2.43)
cat(sprintf("  DR G-comp:  %.3f (OR = %.2f)\n",
    fn_dr(sg)$estimate, exp(fn_dr(sg)$estimate)))
#>   DR G-comp:  1.334 (OR = 3.80)
cat("\nComplement {x1=0} — true log-OR = -0.40:\n")
#> 
#> Complement {x1=0} — true log-OR = -0.40:
cat(sprintf("  Unadjusted: %.3f (OR = %.2f)\n",
    fn_none(co)$estimate, exp(fn_none(co)$estimate)))
#>   Unadjusted: 0.058 (OR = 1.06)
cat(sprintf("  IPTW:       %.3f (OR = %.2f)\n",
    fn_iptw(co)$estimate, exp(fn_iptw(co)$estimate)))
#>   IPTW:       -0.345 (OR = 0.71)
cat(sprintf("  DR G-comp:  %.3f (OR = %.2f)\n",
    fn_dr(co)$estimate, exp(fn_dr(co)$estimate)))
#>   DR G-comp:  -0.011 (OR = 0.99)
ImportantKey Finding

DR G-computation with a treatment-only outcome model (Y ~ treat + ips_covar, no confounders) performs no better than unadjusted estimation because the doubly-robust property requires confounders in the outcome model. IPTW correctly removes confounding bias because it operates through the weights, not the outcome model specification.

6 PS Quality Diagnostics

Show code 
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

for (sc_name in c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F_")) {
  sc_def <- scenarios[[sc_name]]
  df_s <- simulate_obs_study(
    n = 2000, seed = 42L,
    confounding_strength  = sc_def$confounding_strength,
    subgroup_effect       = sc_def$subgroup_effect,
    complement_effect     = sc_def$complement_effect,
    prognostic_strength   = sc_def$prognostic_strength,
    n_noise               = sc_def$n_noise
  )
  all_confs <- c(confs_sim, paste0("noise", seq_len(sc_def$n_noise)))
  ps_s <- estimate_propensity_scores(df_s, "treat", all_confs, method = "grf")

  plot(df_s$ps_true, ps_s$ps_hat, pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = ifelse(df_s$in_sg, "red", "steelblue"),
       xlab = "True PS", ylab = "GRF PS",
       main = paste0(sc_name, ": ", sc_def$name),
       cex.main = 0.7)
  abline(0, 1, col = "black", lwd = 2)
  legend("topleft",
    legend = c(sprintf("cor = %.3f", cor(df_s$ps_true, ps_s$ps_hat)),
               "Subgroup", "Complement"),
    col = c(NA, "red", "steelblue"), pch = c(NA, 16, 16),
    cex = 0.65, bty = "n")
}
Show code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

7 Weight Diagnostics

Show code 
df_strong <- simulate_obs_study(
  n = 2000, seed = 42L,
  confounding_strength = 2.5, prognostic_strength = 1.2,
  subgroup_effect = 1.2, complement_effect = -0.6, n_noise = 3
)
ps_strong <- estimate_propensity_scores(
  df_strong, "treat", c(confs_sim, paste0("noise", 1:3)), method = "grf")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(ps_strong$sw, breaks = 50, col = "#81C784", border = "white",
     main = "Stabilized IPTW Weights", xlab = "sw")
abline(v = 1, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
hist(ps_strong$ips_covar, breaks = 50, col = "#FFE0B2", border = "white",
     main = "IPS Covariate", xlab = "1/f(W|X)")
abline(v = median(ps_strong$ips_covar), col = "red", lwd = 2)
Show code 
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

cat("Stabilized weights:  range [", round(range(ps_strong$sw), 2),
    "], mean =", round(mean(ps_strong$sw), 3), "\n")
#> Stabilized weights:  range [ 0.51 13.26 ], mean = 0.936
Show code 
cat("IPS covariate:       range [", round(range(ps_strong$ips_covar), 2),
    "], median =", round(median(ps_strong$ips_covar), 2), "\n")
#> IPS covariate:       range [ 1.03 27.83 ], median = 1.34

8 Key Principles

  1. IPTW is the recommended default for observational data. It correctly removes confounding bias without requiring confounders in the outcome model, which aligns with ForestSearch’s treatment-only subgroup estimation architecture.

  2. DR G-computation is available but not recommended in ForestSearch’s context. Without confounders in the outcome model, it loses its doubly-robust property and performs no better than unadjusted estimation.

  3. Full-sample PS, used as-is within subgroups. Propensity scores are estimated once on the full df.analysis. The PS is a design quantity; re-estimating within slices would be incorrect.

  4. Bootstrap re-estimates PS from scratch on each resampled dataset.

  5. PS trimming at [2.5%, 97.5%] before computing weights/IPS prevents extreme values.

  6. GRF is the default PS estimator for observational data: non-parametric, cross-fitted via OOB, already computed when use_grf = TRUE.
